title: Key Trends Shaping China's Finished Dosage Formulation Market in 2025–2026
excerpt: China's finished dosage form sector evolves rapidly with a shift towards high-value, complex formulations amid steady market growth and policy support...
content:
China's finished dosage formulation market remains a cornerstone of the global pharmaceutical industry, projected to grow at a CAGR of 7-8% through 2030, driven by chronic diseases, an ageing population and initiatives like Healthy China 2030.

The Asia-Pacific CDMO market, led by China, is valued at ~$60 billion in 2025 with a strong focus on finished dosage forms.

Major Trends

  • Complex Formulations Rise: Increased production of sterile injectables, biosimilars, and controlled-release systems.
  • CDMO Expansion: Outsourcing growth at 8-9% CAGR, with investments in advanced facilities.
  • Regulatory Alignment: NMPA's ICH harmonisation accelerates approvals of innovative finished dosage forms.
  • Digital & Sustainable Practices: AI optimisation and green manufacturing adoption.

These trends solidify China's leadership in affordable, high-quality finished dosage form supply globally.

title: Chinese Finished Dosage Formulations Going Global: Export Growth and International Impact

content:
China strengthens its global pharmaceutical supply role, with finished dosage form exports rising amid quality upgrades and international deals.

Licensing agreements involving Chinese assets accounted for a significant share of global deals in 2025.

Key Developments

  • Export Dominance: Major supplier of generic orals and injectables worldwide.
  • Licensing Surge: Chinese innovative finished dosage forms in ~30-40% of out-licensing deals.
  • Regulated Market Access: Growing approvals for complex generics/biosimilars in US/EU.
  • Resilient Supply: Scale and pricing advantages maintain reliability despite diversification trends.

Supported by Made in China 2025, Chinese finished dosage forms are increasingly vital to global healthcare.

title: China as an Innovator in Finished Dosage Formulations: From Generics to Cutting-Edge Therapies

content:
China transitions from generics leader to innovation hub, contributing about 30% of the global R&D pipeline.

Rapid advancements in high-end finished dosage forms reflect policy and investment shifts.

Innovation Highlights

  • Biosimilars Boom: Numerous mAb biosimilars launched, expanding sterile capabilities.
  • Complex Generics: Progress in controlled-release and specialty products via consistency evaluations.
  • Novel Therapies: ADCs, GLP-1 analogues, and advanced injectables through collaborations.
  • Policy Support: Reforms encourage differentiation and global competitiveness.

China's innovators deliver affordable advanced finished dosage form therapies worldwide.

title: China's API Market in 2025: A $15.97 Billion Industry Poised for Growth
content:
China's Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) market stands as a cornerstone of drug manufacturing worldwide. As we navigate through 2025, this critical sector has reached a significant milestone, valued at USD 15.97 billion and positioned for substantial growth in the coming years. For pharmaceutical professionals monitoring global supply chains, understanding China's evolving role in API production has become essential for strategic planning and market intelligence.

According to comprehensive market analysis from Mordor Intelligence, China's API market is currently valued at USD 15.97 billion in 2025. This robust market is projected to expand at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 7.86% over the next five years, reaching an estimated USD 23.32 billion by 2030. This growth rate significantly outpaces many other pharmaceutical sectors, highlighting the strategic importance of China's API manufacturing capabilities.

The market concentration remains at a medium level, indicating a balance between established players and emerging companies. This competitive landscape has fostered innovation while maintaining sufficient scale economies to keep Chinese APIs cost-competitive on the global stage.

Key Drivers of Market Expansion

Several interconnected factors are propelling the growth of China's API market:

Rising Chronic Disease Burden: China faces significant health challenges that directly drive pharmaceutical demand. Approximately 330 million people in China suffer from cardiovascular diseases, while cancer incidence continues to rise, with projections indicating an increase from 4.8 million new cases in 2022 to 6.85 million by 2040.

Regulatory Transformation: Since December 2023, China has implemented comprehensive drug regulations encompassing various aspects such as API registration renewal, manufacturing outsourcing by marketing authorisation holders (MAHs), and enhanced drug inspection protocols.

Strategic Shift to High-Value APIs: The industry is experiencing a significant transition toward high-value API production, particularly in specialised therapeutic areas. Chinese manufacturers are moving beyond traditional generic API production to develop complex APIs, including high potency APIs, peptides, and specialised therapeutic compounds.

As we progress through 2025, China's $15.97 billion API market stands at a pivotal point of transformation. The strategic shift toward high-value APIs, continued investment in manufacturing capabilities, and regulatory improvements are positioning China to maintain and potentially expand its crucial role in global pharmaceutical supply chains.

title: Regulatory Evolution: How China's New API Policies Are Reshaping the Global Pharmaceutical Landscape
content:
China's regulatory framework for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) has undergone a profound transformation in recent years, culminating in comprehensive reforms implemented in December 2023. These regulatory changes are not merely administrative adjustments but represent a strategic pivot that is reshaping both domestic manufacturing practices and global pharmaceutical supply chains.

The December 2023 Regulatory Overhaul

In December 2023, China implemented its most comprehensive drug regulations to date, introducing sweeping changes to API governance. These regulations addressed several critical areas:

API Registration Renewal Processes: The new framework established more stringent requirements for API registration renewal, emphasising quality consistency evaluation and comprehensive documentation of manufacturing processes.

Manufacturing Outsourcing by Marketing Authorisation Holders (MAHs): The regulations formalised and expanded the MAH system, allowing pharmaceutical companies to outsource manufacturing while retaining regulatory responsibility.

Enhanced Drug Inspection Protocols: The regulatory overhaul introduced risk-based inspection systems with increased frequency and depth of manufacturing site inspections.

NMPA's Transformation and Efficiency Gains

The National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) has emerged as a more efficient and internationally aligned regulatory body. Key developments include:

Accelerated Review Timelines: The NMPA has significantly reduced review times for API registrations, particularly for products addressing unmet medical needs.

International Harmonisation: China's regulatory standards are increasingly aligned with ICH (International Council for Harmonisation) guidelines, facilitating simultaneous global submissions.

China's regulatory transformation in the API sector represents a strategic pivot toward quality, innovation, and international integration. For pharmaceutical professionals, these changes necessitate a reevaluation of sourcing strategies, regulatory approaches, and supply chain management practices.

title: Beyond Generics: China's Strategic Pivot to High-Value API Production
content:
The landscape of China's Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) industry is undergoing a profound transformation. Once primarily known as the world's factory for generic APIs, China is now executing a strategic pivot toward high-value, complex API production. This shift represents not merely an incremental change but a fundamental realignment of the country's pharmaceutical manufacturing capabilities and global market positioning.

The Evolution Beyond Generic APIs

China's API industry has historically dominated the global market for generic pharmaceutical ingredients, leveraging cost advantages, chemical manufacturing infrastructure, and economies of scale. By 2023, China controlled approximately 80% of global generic API supply, establishing itself as an indispensable link in pharmaceutical supply chains worldwide.

However, this dominance in generic APIs, while impressive, came with limitations: thin profit margins, vulnerability to price competition, and limited technological differentiation. Recognising these constraints, China's pharmaceutical sector has been systematically expanding into higher-value API segments.

Growth in Complex Molecules and Specialised APIs

The shift toward high-value APIs is particularly evident in several rapidly expanding segments:

Antibody-Drug Conjugates (ADCs): Chinese manufacturers have made significant inroads into ADC production, one of the most complex and technically demanding areas of API manufacturing.

Peptide APIs: China's peptide API capabilities have expanded dramatically, as exemplified by WuXi TIDES, which supported approximately 50 preclinical to commercial-stage peptide projects in 2023.

China's strategic pivot to high-value API production represents a watershed moment in the global pharmaceutical manufacturing landscape. Moving beyond its established position in generic APIs, China is rapidly developing sophisticated capabilities in complex, high-value pharmaceutical ingredients that are critical components of innovative therapies.

title: Capital Influx: Major Investments Reshaping China's API Manufacturing Capabilities
content:
The Chinese API manufacturing sector is experiencing an unprecedented wave of capital investment, fundamentally transforming the industry's capabilities and global competitive position. These strategic investments are enhancing production capacity, technological sophistication, and quality standards across the API value chain.

Strategic Facility Expansions

Major pharmaceutical companies and contract development and manufacturing organisations (CDMOs) are leading substantial facility expansions:

WuXi AppTec's Taixing Facility: In January 2024, WuXi AppTec established a state-of-the-art API manufacturing facility in Taixing, China, significantly expanding its peptide manufacturing capacity to meet growing global demand. This facility tripled the company's solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS) total reactor volume to 32,000 litres.

AstraZeneca's Production Investment: AstraZeneca announced a USD 26.5 million investment in January 2024 to construct production lines for metformin hydrochloride and dapagliflozin, demonstrating the continued attraction of China's active pharmaceutical ingredients manufacturing sector for global pharmaceutical companies.

These capital investments are not merely expanding production capacity but are fundamentally transforming China's position in the global API value chain, enabling the country to move up the value ladder from basic generic APIs to complex, high-value pharmaceutical ingredients.

title: The Dragon's Grip: How China Dominates Global Pharmaceutical Supply Chains
content:
China's dominance in global pharmaceutical supply chains has reached unprecedented levels, creating both opportunities and challenges for the global healthcare ecosystem. This dominance is particularly pronounced in the Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (API) sector, where China has established itself as the world's primary source for critical pharmaceutical raw materials.

Market Share in Critical Therapeutic Categories

China's control over key API categories has reached levels that make the country an indispensable node in pharmaceutical supply chains:

Analgesics: China produces 90–95% of the ibuprofen imported by the US and EU markets.

Antipyretics: Approximately 70% of the global supply of paracetamol (acetaminophen) originates from Chinese manufacturers.

Antibiotics, Antimicrobials, and Antidiabetics: Critical medicines such as doxycycline, azithromycin and metformin have over 80% import dependency on Chinese sources in many markets.

Competitive Advantages Driving Dominance

Several interconnected factors have enabled China to achieve and maintain this dominant position:

Cost Advantages: Chinese manufacturers can price APIs 35-40% below Western competitors while maintaining FDA/EMA quality standards, creating a compelling value proposition for pharmaceutical companies under pricing pressure.

China's grip on pharmaceutical supply chains represents both a remarkable industrial achievement and a strategic challenge for global healthcare security. As the world continues to grapple with the implications of concentrated API production, China's role as the pharmacy to the world seems likely to endure, even as some diversification efforts gain momentum.

title: The Patent-Cliff Opportunity: How China's API Manufacturers Are Capitalising on Patent Expirations
content:
The pharmaceutical industry is approaching a significant patent cliff, with blockbuster drugs worth many billions of dollars in annual sales facing patent expiry between 2024 and 2028. This wave of patent expirations represents a substantial opportunity for Chinese API manufacturers, who are strategically positioned to capitalise on the resulting surge in generic drug development.

Key Patent Expirations Creating Opportunities

Several high-value medications are losing patent protection in the coming years, creating specific entry points for Chinese API manufacturers:

Apixaban (Eliquis): This anticoagulant medication, which generated over $9 billion in annual sales, faces patent expiration. Chinese API manufacturers have already developed bioequivalent API production processes and are poised to supply generic manufacturers globally.

Dabigatran (Pradaxa): Another anticoagulant losing patent protection, creating opportunities in a high-value therapeutic area where Chinese manufacturers have developed specialised expertise.

The patent cliff represents a pivotal opportunity for Chinese API manufacturers to further consolidate their global market position while moving up the value chain. By strategically targeting high-value molecules coming off patent, these companies are positioning themselves not merely as suppliers of basic pharmaceutical ingredients but as sophisticated partners in the development of affordable medicines worldwide.

title: Disease Demographics: How China's Health Challenges Drive API Innovation
content:
China's evolving disease burden is creating a powerful domestic driver for pharmaceutical innovation, particularly in the Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (API) sector. The country's demographic and epidemiological transitions are reshaping the landscape of pharmaceutical demand, creating both challenges for the healthcare system and opportunities for API manufacturers.

Cardiovascular Disease Burden

Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) have emerged as the leading cause of mortality and morbidity in China, creating substantial demand for related APIs:

According to a study published in March 2023, approximately 330 million people were suffering from cardiovascular diseases in China, with conditions like coronary heart disease, stroke, atrial fibrillation, and pulmonary heart disease being most prevalent.

This enormous patient population has driven significant expansion in API production for antihypertensives, statins, anticoagulants, and other cardiovascular medications. Chinese manufacturers have responded by increasing production capacity for key cardiovascular APIs, including atorvastatin, clopidogrel, and valsartan.

Rising Cancer Incidence

Cancer represents another major driver of pharmaceutical demand and API innovation in China:

According to projections published in February 2022, approximately 4.8 million new cancer cases were expected to be reported in China in 2022, with this number projected to increase to 6.85 million new cancer cases by 2040.

China's disease demographics are creating a powerful impetus for API innovation and manufacturing expansion. As the country continues to grapple with the rising burden of chronic diseases, its pharmaceutical industry is responding with increased investment in API production capabilities, particularly for medications targeting cardiovascular disease, cancer, and neurodegenerative conditions.

title: Biological Revolution: China's Emerging Leadership in Biologic APIs
content:
China's biopharmaceutical sector is undergoing a remarkable transformation, with rapid advances in biological Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) positioning the country as an emerging leader in this high-value segment. Once primarily focused on small molecule APIs, China is now making significant inroads into the more complex and technically demanding field of biological APIs.

Biosimilar Development and Approval

China has made remarkable progress in biosimilar development and commercialisation:

According to an article published by JAMA Network Open in October 2023, as of February 2023, the Chinese regulatory authority had approved approximately 20 biosimilars developed by local companies, making China one of the leading biosimilar producers after the United States and Europe.

This growing portfolio of approved biosimilars demonstrates China's increasing capabilities in biological API manufacturing, including the complex processes required for protein expression, purification, and characterisation.

Strategic Investments and Partnerships

The biological API sector in China has attracted substantial investment and strategic partnerships:

In January 2024, Biogen and Eisai's Leqembi received approval from China's National Medical Products Administration, making China the third country after the United States and Japan to approve this antibody-based therapeutic for Alzheimer's disease treatment.

China's emergence as a significant player in biological APIs represents a new chapter in the country's pharmaceutical evolution. Moving beyond its established strength in small molecule APIs, China is developing sophisticated capabilities in protein-based therapeutics, positioning itself to compete in one of the highest-value segments of the pharmaceutical industry.

title: Sustainable Synthesis: Green Chemistry Initiatives in China's API Industry
content:
China's Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) industry is undergoing a significant transformation toward sustainability, with green chemistry initiatives gaining momentum across the sector. This shift represents both a response to regulatory pressures and a strategic positioning for competitive advantage in an increasingly environmentally conscious global market.

Regulatory Drivers of Sustainability

China's regulatory environment has become increasingly focused on environmental protection, creating powerful incentives for API manufacturers to adopt sustainable practices:

The Environmental Protection Law amendments and pharmaceutical-specific environmental regulations have established stringent standards for waste management, emissions control, and resource utilisation in API manufacturing.

These regulations have been accompanied by robust enforcement mechanisms, including substantial fines, production restrictions, and even facility closures for non-compliant manufacturers.

Green Chemistry Adoption

In response to regulatory pressures and market opportunities, Chinese API manufacturers are increasingly adopting green chemistry principles:

Solvent Reduction and Recycling: Leading manufacturers have implemented solvent recovery systems that achieve recycling rates of 80-90% for common organic solvents, significantly reducing both environmental impact and production costs.

The sustainability transformation in China's API industry represents a significant evolution in the country's pharmaceutical manufacturing approach. What began largely as a response to regulatory pressure has evolved into a strategic differentiator, with sustainable manufacturing practices increasingly viewed as essential for long-term competitiveness in global markets.

title: Digital Transformation: How AI Is Revolutionising API Development in China
content:
China's Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) industry is experiencing a profound digital transformation, with artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced analytics revolutionising both research and manufacturing processes. This technological evolution is enabling unprecedented efficiency, quality, and innovation in API development, positioning China at the forefront of pharmaceutical manufacturing's digital future.

AI-Driven API Discovery and Development

Artificial intelligence is transforming the early stages of API development in China:

Predictive Modelling: Chinese pharmaceutical companies are deploying sophisticated AI algorithms to predict molecular properties, stability, and synthesis routes for novel APIs. These models can evaluate thousands of potential compounds in silico, dramatically accelerating the identification of promising candidates.

Retrosynthesis Planning: AI-powered retrosynthesis tools are enabling researchers to identify optimal synthesis pathways for complex APIs, considering factors such as yield, cost, safety, and environmental impact. Companies like XtalPi and Insilico Medicine have developed platforms that can generate multiple synthetic routes and rank them based on feasibility and efficiency.

Manufacturing Process Optimisation

Beyond discovery, AI is revolutionising API manufacturing processes:

Process Analytical Technology (PAT): Advanced sensors combined with machine learning algorithms are enabling real-time monitoring and control of API manufacturing processes. These systems can detect subtle deviations from optimal parameters and make immediate adjustments, improving consistency and reducing batch failures.

The digital transformation of China's API industry represents a step-change in pharmaceutical manufacturing capabilities. By embracing AI, advanced analytics, and automation, Chinese manufacturers are not merely improving efficiency but fundamentally reimagining how APIs are discovered, developed, and produced.

title: Cooperation & Competition: China's API Industry on the World Stage
content:
The global Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) landscape is characterised by a complex interplay of cooperation and competition, with China occupying a central but evolving position. As geopolitical considerations increasingly influence pharmaceutical supply chains, China's API industry is navigating a changing international environment that presents both challenges and opportunities.

China-India API Dynamics

The relationship between the world's two largest API producers is marked by both competition and complementarity:

Comparative Advantages: China has maintained dominance in chemical synthesis and raw material production, controlling approximately 80% of global generic API supply by volume. India, meanwhile, has leveraged its FDA-approved facilities (the highest number outside the U.S.) and strong formulation capabilities to become the "pharmacy of the world" for finished dosage forms.

Strategic Shifts: India's Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme aims to boost domestic API production, targeting self-reliance by 2025 and reducing imports from China by 35%. This initiative represents one of the most significant attempts to reshape API supply chains globally.

Western Reshoring Initiatives

Developed economies are increasingly pursuing pharmaceutical supply chain diversification:

Policy Measures: Both the United States and European Union have implemented initiatives to encourage domestic API production, including US domestic-manufacturing initiatives and the EU Pharmaceutical Strategy. These measures combine financial incentives, regulatory preferences, and strategic investments to reduce dependency on Chinese APIs.

The global API landscape is entering a period of significant recalibration, with China's dominant position being challenged by both competitive pressures and strategic diversification efforts. However, the fundamental advantages that enabled China's rise in API manufacturing—cost efficiency, chemical expertise, and manufacturing scale—remain largely intact.

title: 2030 Vision: The Future of China's API Industry
content:
As we look toward 2030, China's Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) industry stands at an inflection point, with transformative forces reshaping its trajectory. Current projections indicate a market size reaching $23.32 billion by 2030, representing a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 7.86% from 2025. However, the qualitative evolution of the industry may prove even more significant than its quantitative growth.

Market Size and Growth Projections

The expansion of China's API market is expected to continue robustly through 2030:

According to Mordor Intelligence analysis, the market is projected to grow from $15.97 billion in 2025 to $23.32 billion by 2030, maintaining a CAGR of 7.86% throughout this period.

This growth will be driven by both volume expansion in established API categories and value growth from the increasing proportion of complex, high-value APIs in the product mix.

Technological Evolution

The technological landscape of API manufacturing in China is expected to undergo significant transformation by 2030:

Continuous Manufacturing Dominance: By 2030, continuous manufacturing is projected to account for over 30% of API production in China, up from less than 10% in 2025. This shift will enable higher efficiency, improved quality consistency, and reduced environmental impact.

As we approach 2030, China's API industry is poised for both quantitative growth and qualitative transformation. The projected market size of $23.32 billion represents not merely an expansion of existing capabilities but the emergence of a more sophisticated, innovation-driven, and globally integrated industry.

title: How to register a medicine in Iran: a practical guide for foreign manufacturers
excerpt: Foreign medicines reach Iran through an IFDA-licensed importer that registers the product, imports it and keeps it on the market. What the route looks like, which documents matter and where projects usually stall.
content:
Every medicine sold in Iran needs a registration with the Iran Food and Drug Administration (IFDA). A foreign manufacturer cannot hold that registration itself: it works through an Iranian company licensed by IFDA to import medicines, which files the dossier, receives the product's IRC code, imports, and remains responsible for the product on the market.

1. Choose the importer first

The importer becomes your registration holder in practice. Look for a company that already holds an IFDA import licence, has its own regulatory staff, can run pharmacovigilance, and has a distribution route to hospitals and pharmacies. Agree in writing who does what: dossier, pricing file, import permits, storage, recalls and complaints. The manufacturer then issues a letter of authorisation (LoA) naming that importer for the product.

2. Prepare the dossier

  • CTD dossier (modules 1–5 as applicable): quality data for the API and the finished product, stability for the intended shelf life and climate, and clinical or bioequivalence data where required.
  • Proof of registration in the country of origin, usually a Certificate of Pharmaceutical Product (CPP) or free-sale certificate.
  • GMP evidence for the manufacturing site; IFDA may ask for an inspection or rely on a recognised authority's certificate.
  • Artwork and labelling that can carry the Persian label and patient leaflet required for the Iranian market.

3. Registration, pricing and IRC

The importer submits the file to IFDA, answers questions and prepares the pricing file. When the product is approved it receives an IRC code, which then appears on every pack and is used for tracking in the Iranian supply chain.

4. Emergency import as a faster first step

For medicines in shortage or not yet registered, IFDA allows emergency (فوریتی) import by licensed importers against a defined need. It is a practical way to supply the market while the full registration is in progress, but it is not a substitute for it.

5. Where projects usually stall

  • A CPP or GMP certificate that has expired or does not match the exact product and site in the dossier.
  • Stability data that do not cover the shelf life or climatic zone being claimed.
  • No agreed responsibility for pharmacovigilance and recalls between manufacturer and importer.
  • Choosing an importer without regulatory staff, so questions from IFDA go unanswered for months.

Local manufacturing under licence

Iran manufactures most of the medicines it uses, and policy favours local production. For many products the stronger long-term route is manufacture under licence by an Iranian GMP plant, with the foreign company keeping the brand and the quality standard. See licensed manufacturing in Iran.

title: Exporting APIs to Iran: what Iranian manufacturers ask their suppliers for
excerpt: Iran has a large domestic pharmaceutical industry that imports most of its active ingredients. What buyers check before ordering, which documents decide the deal, and how the import works.
content:
Iran produces most of its own finished medicines, but the active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) behind them are largely imported, with China and India the main sources. For an API manufacturer this makes Iran a market of many industrial buyers rather than a single tender, and the buyers are technical: their quality and regulatory teams decide before purchasing does.

What buyers check first

  • The API's regulatory file: an open part of a DMF, a CEP or an equivalent technical package, so the Iranian manufacturer can add the source to its own product registration at IFDA.
  • GMP certificate of the manufacturing site, current and matching the site that will make the batches.
  • Certificate of analysis against the pharmacopoeia the buyer works to (USP, EP or BP), and samples for testing.
  • Stability data and the retest period.
  • Route of synthesis and impurity profile, including residual solvents and, increasingly, nitrosamine risk assessment.

Why a new source takes time

Changing or adding an API source is a variation to the finished product's registration. The buyer must test samples, often run trial batches and stability, and file the change with IFDA before commercial orders follow. Suppliers that send a complete technical package at the start shorten this step considerably.

How the import works

APIs are imported by companies licensed by IFDA for pharmaceutical raw materials. The importer obtains the import permit for each consignment against the documents above, arranges customs clearance and quality release, and delivers to the manufacturer. Controlled substances and precursors need additional licences.

What helps a supplier win business

  • A clear specification sheet and CoA in English, matched to the pharmacopoeia the buyer uses.
  • Willingness to share the open part of the DMF and to answer quality questionnaires.
  • Consistent quality across batches, with change notifications sent in advance.
  • An importer in Iran who knows both the buyer's technical requirements and the IFDA process.

title: ICH M4Q(R2): how the new quality part of the CTD differs from M4Q(R1)
excerpt: The revision of ICH M4Q is the first major change to the quality part of the CTD since 2002. A side-by-side view of M4Q(R1) and the M4Q(R2) draft: the role of Module 2.3, the new structure of Module 3, lifecycle management and what to prepare now.
content:
The quality part of the Common Technical Document, defined in ICH M4Q, has barely changed since M4Q(R1) was finalised in 2002. Its revision, M4Q(R2), reached Step 2 in May 2025 and went out for consultation in the ICH regions; the final guideline (Step 4) is planned for 2027, after which each region will set its own implementation date. The draft changes both the role of the summary and the organisation of the data.

The core idea

In M4Q(R1), Module 3 holds the information and Module 2.3, the Quality Overall Summary, repeats it in shorter form, section by section. In the M4Q(R2) draft the relationship is reversed: Module 2.3 becomes the place where the key quality information, the control strategy and its justification are presented and assessed, and Module 3 holds the supporting data.

Module 3: from a fixed list to a modular structure

M4Q(R1) uses one fixed list of headings for the drug substance (3.2.S.1–S.7) and one for the drug product (3.2.P.1–P.8), with appendices for facilities, adventitious agents and novel excipients. Products that do not fit, such as drug-device combinations or multiple intermediates, are placed wherever they fit best. The draft R2 gives every material its own place and the same order inside it.

Side by side

M4Q(R1) (2002)M4Q(R2) draft (2025)
Role of Module 2.3Summary of Module 3, about 40 pagesMain presentation of the quality case; basis of the assessment
Control strategySpread across S.2, S.4, P.2, P.3 and P.5Presented as a whole in 2.3.2
Development knowledgeMainly P.2 (pharmaceutical development)Development summary and justifications for substance and product (2.3.4)
LifecycleNot addressed in the structureOwn section (2.3.5) using ICH Q12 tools such as established conditions and post-approval change management protocols
Benefit-riskNo place for itOptional product quality benefit-risk section (2.3.6)
Module 3 organisationTwo fixed lists (S and P) plus appendicesOne block per material with a repeated order
Complex productsFitted into existing headingsIntermediates, excipients and device constituents have their own place
Regional information3.2.RAddendum
Link to other ICH guidelinesWritten before ICH Q8–Q12Built on ICH Q8–Q12 concepts

What this means for sponsors and manufacturers

  • Module 2.3 can no longer be written at the end. The control strategy and its justification have to be clear during development, because they will be presented as the core of the dossier.
  • Development knowledge becomes submission content. Risk assessments, design space and the reasoning behind specifications should be kept in a form that can go into 2.3.2 and 2.3.4.
  • Lifecycle is planned at filing. Deciding which elements are established conditions, and how they may change, becomes part of the first submission.
  • Existing dossiers are not converted yet. Regions have not published implementation rules; plan new applications first and follow the Step 4 text, as details may still change from the draft.

Hanpars prepares and reviews CTD quality dossiers and helps teams plan the move to the new structure. See CTD/eCTD dossiers and IMPD.

title: How to answer a deficiency letter: the questions agencies ask most and how to close them
excerpt: A list of questions or a deficiency letter is a normal part of assessment. How to sort the questions, decide what needs new data, and write answers that an assessor can close in one round.
content:
Almost no marketing authorisation application is approved without questions. The EMA sends lists of questions at defined points of the procedure, the FDA issues information requests and complete response letters, and national authorities send deficiency letters. The quality of the answers, not the number of questions, decides whether the application moves on or goes into another round.

The questions agencies ask most

  • Specifications: limits not justified by batch data, missing tests, or limits wider than the pharmacopoeia or the reference product.
  • Impurities: unqualified impurities, missing nitrosamine risk assessment, residual solvents and elemental impurities (ICH Q3C, Q3D).
  • Stability: too few batches or months of data, the wrong climatic zone, or a shelf life longer than the data supports.
  • Manufacturing process: incomplete process description, missing process validation or critical process parameters without justification.
  • Bioequivalence: choice of reference product, statistical analysis, or a biowaiver that does not meet the criteria.
  • Consistency: data that differ between Module 2 and Module 3, or between the dossier and the GMP documents.
  • Product information: wording of the SmPC or leaflet that does not match the data or the reference product.

A method that works

  1. Classify every question: major objection or other concern, quality, non-clinical or clinical, and whether it needs new data, a better justification, or a correction.
  2. Plan the timeline: new stability or analytical data take time. Check the response deadline and whether an extension of the clock stop is possible before promising anything.
  3. Answer the question that was asked: restate the question, give a direct answer in the first sentence, then the evidence, with references to the exact dossier section.
  4. Update the dossier: every change promised in the answer must appear in the updated Module 3 or product information, submitted in the same sequence.
  5. Review from the assessor's side: before sending, read each answer as the assessor will and ask whether it can be closed without another question.

Common mistakes

  • Long general text that does not answer the point.
  • Commitments to provide data later where the agency expects the data now.
  • Answers that create new inconsistencies with other modules.
  • Arguing against a guideline instead of justifying a deviation with data.

Hanpars reviews dossiers before submission and prepares responses to agency questions. See dossier review and deficiency responses.

title: Preparing for an EU-GMP or PIC/S inspection: a mock-inspection checklist
excerpt: A GMP certificate from a recognised authority is often a condition for registration in a new market. What inspectors look at first, how to run a mock inspection, and the findings that come up most often.
content:
For a manufacturer outside Europe, an EU-GMP inspection or an inspection by a PIC/S member authority is often the step that decides whether a product can be registered in a new market. The inspection itself lasts a few days; the preparation decides the result.

What inspectors look at first

  • The Site Master File and the list of products and processes in scope.
  • The pharmaceutical quality system: change control, deviations, CAPA, complaints, recalls and product quality reviews.
  • Validation status: process, cleaning, analytical methods, equipment and computerised systems.
  • Data integrity in the laboratory: audit trails, access rights, raw data and how out-of-specification results are handled.
  • Contamination control, especially for sterile products under the revised EU GMP Annex 1.
  • Supplier qualification for APIs and critical materials.

Running a mock inspection

  1. Define the scope as the real inspection will: authority, products, dosage forms and the date.
  2. Use an independent team that did not write the procedures, and follow the authority's own inspection approach.
  3. Test the front room and back room: how fast documents are found, who answers which questions, and how requests are tracked.
  4. Walk the process from receipt of materials to release, and trace a few batches through records, deviations and changes.
  5. Write graded findings (critical, major, other) as the inspector would, with a corrective action plan, owner and date for each.

Findings that come up most often

  • Deviations closed without a convincing root cause, and CAPA that do not prevent recurrence.
  • Audit trails not reviewed, or shared user accounts on laboratory systems.
  • Out-of-specification investigations that invalidate results without evidence.
  • Cleaning validation that does not cover worst-case products or equipment.
  • Gaps between the registered process in the dossier and what is done on the floor.

After the inspection

Answer each finding within the authority's deadline with a root-cause analysis, corrective and preventive actions and evidence of completion. A well-closed inspection gives a certificate that can be used in several registrations.

Members of our team have hosted EU-GMP, MHRA, ANVISA, Minpromtorg and TİTCK inspections. See GMP inspection readiness.

title: Drug registration routes compared: EU, UK, EAEU, GCC and Türkiye
excerpt: Who can apply, which procedures exist and how long assessment takes in five markets that are often planned together: the EU, the United Kingdom, the Eurasian Economic Union, the Gulf states and Türkiye.
content:
Manufacturers that plan several markets often reuse one dossier, but the routes, the local requirements and the timelines differ. This is an overview of five markets that are often planned together. Timelines are the authorities' assessment targets and do not include the time the applicant needs to answer questions.

European Union

  • Routes: centralised procedure at the EMA (one authorisation for all member states, mandatory for biotechnology products and some new active substances), decentralised and mutual recognition procedures, and national procedures.
  • Applicant: the marketing authorisation holder must be established in the EU/EEA, with a QPPV and EU batch release.
  • Timeline: 210 days of assessment for the centralised and decentralised procedures, plus clock stops.

United Kingdom

  • Routes: the International Recognition Procedure, which relies on an approval by a reference regulator (Recognition A in 60 days, Recognition B in 110 days), and the 150-day national assessment.
  • Applicant: established in the UK or the EU/EEA. New licences cover the whole of the UK.

Eurasian Economic Union

  • Routes: registration under the common EAEU rules with a reference state, which assesses the dossier, and concerned states, which recognise its report (mutual recognition or decentralised).
  • Applicant: an authorised representative registered in the filing state. Product information in Russian.
  • GMP: an EAEU GMP inspection, which under current rules can follow within three years of registration.

Gulf states

  • Routes: the GCC centralised procedure of the Gulf Health Council, followed by national certificates and prices, or national registration in each country.
  • Applicant: a local agent; in Saudi Arabia also a Saudi-based pharmacovigilance person.
  • Reliance: the SFDA has verification and abridged reviews for eligible products approved by the FDA or EMA.

Türkiye

  • Applicant: a licence holder resident in Türkiye.
  • Timeline: a 210-day licensing period, with processes starting in February, May, August and November.
  • GMP: a TİTCK GMP certificate for foreign sites, based on inspection or reliance; price approval and reimbursement are separate steps.

Planning several markets

Start with the market whose approval helps the others, usually the EU or the UK because of reliance routes elsewhere. Write Module 3 once, to the strictest expectations, and plan the GMP inspections early: they are often the longest step.

See drug registration by country for the markets we support, including where a local partner or agent is needed.

title: Biosimilar comparability: what agencies expect in the dossier
excerpt: A biosimilar is approved on the strength of its comparability to the reference product. What the analytical package must show, how much clinical data is still expected, and where dossiers are usually challenged.
content:
A biosimilar does not have to repeat the full development of the reference product. It has to show that it is highly similar in quality, with no clinically meaningful differences in safety and efficacy. The evidence for that is built step by step, and the analytical comparison carries most of the weight.

The stepwise approach

  1. Analytical similarity: structure, physicochemical properties and biological activity compared with several batches of the reference product.
  2. Non-clinical data: mainly in-vitro functional assays; animal studies are now rarely expected.
  3. Clinical data: pharmacokinetic and, where needed, pharmacodynamic comparison. Agencies increasingly accept that a comparative efficacy trial may not be needed when the analytical and PK data are strong.

What the analytical package must show

  • Primary structure and higher-order structure.
  • Glycosylation, charge variants, size variants and other product-related substances and impurities.
  • Biological activity through assays that reflect the mechanism of action, including Fc-related functions for antibodies.
  • Enough reference product batches, over time, to set meaningful similarity ranges.
  • A justification for every difference found, showing that it has no clinical impact.

Where dossiers are challenged

  • Similarity ranges based on too few reference batches or set without statistical reasoning.
  • Differences in glycosylation or potency explained only in words, without functional data.
  • Changes in the manufacturing process during development without a comparability exercise (ICH Q5E).
  • Use of a reference product sourced from another region without a bridge.

After approval

Every later process, site or scale change needs its own comparability assessment under ICH Q5E, and a comparability protocol agreed in advance can make these changes faster.

Hanpars designs and reviews the regulatory side of biosimilar programmes. See development strategy and study plans.

title: Dossier gap analysis before submission: a module-by-module checklist
excerpt: Most questions in assessment could have been predicted. A practical checklist for reviewing a dossier before it goes to the agency, module by module.
content:
A gap analysis compares the dossier with what the target agency will expect, before the agency sees it. It is most useful when a dossier written for one region is used for another, when the product or process has changed since the dossier was written, or before the first submission to a strict authority.

Module 1

  • All regional forms and declarations, in the current version.
  • Product information that matches the data and, for generics, the reference product.
  • GMP evidence for every site named in the dossier.

Module 2

  • Every statement in the summaries can be traced to data in Modules 3 to 5.
  • Figures, specifications and batch numbers match the data modules exactly.

Module 3: drug substance

  • A current DMF/ASMF or CEP with a letter of access, and specifications aligned with it.
  • Impurity profile, residual solvents, elemental impurities and nitrosamine risk assessment.
  • Stability data and retest period.

Module 3: drug product

  • Pharmaceutical development that justifies the formulation and process.
  • Process description and validation (or a validation scheme where allowed) for the commercial scale.
  • Specifications justified by batch data and current pharmacopoeia.
  • Stability data for the climatic zone of the target market, and container closure suitability.

Modules 4 and 5

  • For generics: bioequivalence against a reference product accepted in the target market, or a justified biowaiver.
  • For literature-based applications: references that are current and actually support the claims.

Turning findings into a plan

Rate each gap by risk (likely major objection, minor question, cosmetic), decide whether it needs new data, a justification or an editorial fix, and assign an owner and date. Close the high-risk gaps before submission; record the rest so the team is ready for the questions.

Hanpars carries out dossier gap analysis and pre-assessment from the assessor's point of view. See dossier review and deficiency responses.

title: The IMPD under the EU Clinical Trials Regulation: quality section essentials
excerpt: Since the EU Clinical Trials Regulation applies to all trials, the IMPD is submitted through CTIS as part of a single application. What the quality section must cover and where applications are commonly questioned.
content:
The Investigational Medicinal Product Dossier (IMPD) describes the quality of every investigational product used in a clinical trial, and where needed its non-clinical and clinical data. Under the EU Clinical Trials Regulation (Regulation (EU) No 536/2014), the IMPD is submitted through the Clinical Trials Information System (CTIS) as part of one application assessed jointly by the member states concerned.

Full or simplified IMPD

A full IMPD is needed for a product with no marketing authorisation in the EU. A simplified IMPD can be used when the product, or a product with the same active substance, is already authorised or has been described in an earlier application, with references instead of repeated data.

What the quality section covers

  • Drug substance: manufacturer, manufacturing process outline, characterisation, specifications, batch analyses and stability.
  • Drug product: composition, manufacturing, control of excipients, specifications, batch analyses and stability supporting the proposed shelf life.
  • Placebo and comparators: composition and, for modified comparators, data showing that the change does not affect performance.
  • GMP: manufacturing and import authorisations, and a QP declaration for products made outside the EU.

Phase-appropriate expectations

Requirements grow with the phase of development. Early-phase IMPDs can use wider, provisional specifications and less stability data, but the safety-related aspects, such as impurities, sterility and viral safety for biologics, are expected from the start.

Where applications are questioned

  • Specifications without a link to the batches used in non-clinical studies.
  • Shelf-life extensions without a stability protocol.
  • Missing information on changes between the batches used in earlier and current trials.
  • Comparator products repackaged or blinded without supporting data.

Hanpars prepares quality IMPDs and supports clinical trial applications. See CTD/eCTD dossiers and IMPD.
